text:
The Census
Decennial Census: Mandated by the Constitution, conducted every 10 years with 10 questions.
American Community Survey (ACS): Created in 2005, more interesting questions! Approximately 3% of households are surveyed about income, rent, home value, commute time, ethnicity, etc. From that sample, we come up with an estimate for the population.

1-year ACS: Almost never used, only for places > 65,000 people. Most current, comes out every year.
5-year ACS: Block Group, Census Tract. If you get ACS data for the year 2016, it is a 5 year average. These are estimates +- a margin of error. It is NOT just an estimate for 2016, but for the interval of 2011-2016.


Census Code

B19013_001E or B19013_001M

B: Base table
19013: Table #
001: Line Number
E: Estimate
M: Margin of Error

The command load_variables() shows us the name of our variables. All of this exists in a library called tidycensus().



Census Geography

State -> County -> Tract (“Neighborhood”) -> Block Groups (HORRIBLE margins of error!) -> Block (Decennial Census only)
About 5,000-8,000 people
Boundaries of census tracts change over time! To mitigate this, there are longitudinal tract databases



GEOID
A GEOID is a unique identifier for a census tract.

First two numbers is the state
Next three numbers is the county
Last six digits are the census tract

A GEOID is stored as string. This is important, as there are states such as Alabama with a 01 state identifier.


Using tidycensus()

data <- get_acs(geography: 'county',
                variables = c('B1013_001',
                              'B01003_001'),
                state = 'PA',
                year = 2023,
                survey = 'acs5',
                output = 'wide') #To get our data in wide format 

When we run this command, we receive it in tidy format, with multiple rows for each county (each row shows a different variable value –> “variable” itself is a column). We want to turn it into wide format, with different variables in each column.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I look at total commuters across counties in Connecticut, and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably. As Connecticut features a large commuter region to New York in the southwestern part of the state, I am curious about the general patterns across Connecticut and where census estimates tend to be more reliable.

How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Sorting counties into reliability categories

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 1  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 2 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence     1
2 Low confidence      2
3 Moderate            6


As the percent margin of error for all 9 planning regions of Connecticut fell well into the original <5% cutoff for High confidence, the categories were adjusted so that High confidence represents a margin of error of <1%, Moderate represents a margin of error of <2%, and Low confidence represents a margin of error of >2%.

section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                                          myvarE myvarM   popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                                          <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1 09110 Capitol Planning Region, Connecticut          411729   3849 969029    NA
2 09120 Greater Bridgeport Planning Region, Connecti… 136932   2110 326296    NA
3 09130 Lower Connecticut River Valley Planning Regi…  78097   1309 174983    NA
4 09140 Naugatuck Valley Planning Region, Connecticut 198589   2586 452303    NA
5 09150 Northeastern Connecticut Planning Region, Co…  42707   1095  95829    NA
6 09160 Northwest Hills Planning Region, Connecticut   49420   1043 112848    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 1  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 2 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(avg_population))

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence          1        969029 
2 Moderate                 6        403440.
3 Low confidence           2        104338.


The avg_population of high-confidence planning regions are much higher than the avg_population of low-confidence planning regions, the former being about 969,029 and the latter being about 104,338.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
Through this exercise, we learned that we know the least about the Northeastern Connecticut and the Northeast Hills planning regions. As both of these planning regions feature the lowest populations in the state, they feature the lowest sample sizes and largest percent margin of error (>2%) in the American Community Survey data set.
It is important to understand the variability of reliability within the ACS data set when making policy decisions, as certain planning regions with lower sample sizes may be underrepresented. For example, communities in the northeastern and northwestern corners of the state may appear to have fewer commuters than in the Hartford region, though in reality it may be an artifact of sample size. Poor data literacy in the policy making process could result in a reduction in bus service within these regions, despite them in reality having a larger need for public transportation than anticipated.

text:
Cleaning up an ugly chart
There are numerous things we can do to a default chart to make it more readable.
arrange() and slice_head() trims down the amount of data in the chart.

arrange(desc(moe_pct)) |> 
  slice_head(n=15)

coord_flip() turns a chart on its side.
(aes(x = reorder(NAME, estimate), y = estimate)) reorders the \(x\) axis by estimate, rather than alphabetically.
mutate(NAME = str_remove(NAME, " County, New York")) rewrites name of string values in a column by removing " County, New York" from the county name – so "Nassau County, New York" becomes "Nassau".
geom_errorbar(aes(...), width = 0.3) changes the width of the error bars.
Adding fill = 'steelblue' to geom_bar() and theme_minimal() will provide a new theme to the graph.
scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) adds commas to numbers on the \(y\) axis.
labs() allows us to add labels to the plot.

title: Week 3: Margins of error and ggplot2
text:
Margin of Error
The census does not use the percent margin of error in its estimates. Instead, it uses the Coefficient of Variation (CV).
It is the relative measure of sampling error:
\[\text{CV}=\frac{\text{Standard Error}}{\text{estimate}} \times 100\]
Standard Errors come from a calculation of how many people you asked, and how varied that sample is. To get a standard error using a 90% confidence interval:
\[\text{Standard Error} = \frac{\text{Margin of Error }(E)}{1.645}\]
For a sample of 10,000:

15% CV -> High reliability
15-30% CV -> Medium reliability
30% CV -> Low reliability; High sampling error


Derived Uncertainty
\[\text{Poverty rate}=\frac{\text{\# in Poverty}\pm E}{\text{Total Population}\pm E} \]


In R:
moe_sum(): adding estimates together
moe_prop(): one estimate as share of another
moe_ratio(): # in Poverty/HH income; one is not a subset of another


Change over Time

Overlapping intervals 2019-2023, 2018, 2022
Non-overlapping intervals 2014-2018, 2019-2023

We can’t take the difference between estimates as the absolute change between intervals without taking into account margin of error \(E\).


The Standard Error of Difference
\[SE_{\text{diff}}=\sqrt{(SE_1)^2 +(SE_2)^2}\]






NoteExample




2014-2018: $45,000 \(\pm\) 8,000
2019-2023: $62,000 \(\pm\) 11,000

We want to know if these estimates are truly different from one another.
\[SE_{\text{diff}}=\sqrt{(\frac{8{,}000}{1.645})^2+(\frac{11{,}000}{1.645})^2} \approx 8,626\]
\[\text{Difference}=\pm(1.645\times SE_{\text{diff}})\]
\[\text{Interval}=17{,}000\pm (1.645 \times 8{,}268)=17{,}000\pm13{,}601 =[3{,}399,\ 30{,}601]\]
\[Z = \frac{62{,}000-45{,}000}{SE_{\text{diff}}} \approx 2.06 \]
Since the 90% confidence interval for the difference \([3{,}399,\ 30{,}601]\) doesn’t contain zero (equivalently, \(Z \approx 2.06 > 1.645\)), we can say with 90% confidence that the estimate genuinely increased from 2014–2018 to 2019–2023.


Code from the practice exercise:

poverty_tested <- poverty_wide %>%
  mutate(
    change   = `estimate_2019-2023` - `estimate_2014-2018`,
    se_1     = `moe_2014-2018` / 1.645,
    se_2     = `moe_2019-2023` / 1.645,
    se_diff  = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,
    z        = change / se_diff,
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645
  )

Example:
Take a census tract where bike usage goes from 25% to 20% between the 2023 and 2015 5YE.
The moe in the data is tied to the 90% confidence interval. It’s the range of values where the true, unknown value lives.

It’s important to know that we can’t just add the margins of errors. We need to convert it to the standard error \(SE\). For our example:
\[
SE_{2015}=\frac{3}{1.645}=1.82
\]
\[
SE_{2023}=\frac{4}{1.645}=2.43
\]
To get the difference of the standard errors:
\[
SE_{\text{diff}}=\sqrt{SE_{2015}^2+SE_{2023}^2} = 3.04
\]
\[
Z=\frac{25-20}{3.04}=1.64
\]
Since \(1.64 \le 1.645\), we cannot reject \(H_0\) that the difference is due to sampling noise.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data
text:
Coordinate Reference Systems (CRS)
When you request census data through this method:

get_acs(..., geometry=TRUE)

It adds a geometry column with geometric data in a coordinate reference system!

Geographic CRS
The true shape of the earth is a lumpy geoid and we can’t really put a grid on it. Instead, we approximate the shape of the Earth with an ellipsoid. There can be many types of ellipsoids.
No matter how we draw an ellipsoid, it’s never going to perfectly match the geoid.
Lines of latitude and longitude derived from a specific ellipsoid can be referred to as a datum or a geographic coordinate reference system. For example, the North American Datum of 1983 (NAD83) has the ellipsoid of GRS-80. Whenever coordinates are given in latitude/longitude, they are from a geographic CRS.
The World Geodetic Datum of 1984 (WGS84), like NAD83, is Earth-centered via satellites. It is the standard for GPS data and is global (rather than NAD83, though it is not that far off).
However, when you’re doing spatial analysis, you are typically not going to measure in degrees.


Projected CRS
When we project a 3D object onto a 2D object, the shapes, area, distance, and direction will be distorted. All projected CRS start out with a 3D model of the Earth which then will be flattened.
The issue is that the flat surface will not touch all of the parts of the Earth perfectly. Where the Earth touches the projection, it will be projected perfectly. Everywhere else will be projected larger and distorted. The tangent line is where there is the least distortion.
The Mercator projection is cylindrical, and areas closer to the poles have extreme size distortion. Conic projections are better for countries like Russia and Canada at higher latitudes. Transverse cylindrical projections run along lines of longitude, and are better for continents like the Americas that are very long north-south. Planar or azimuthal projections are good for the poles.


Choosing a CRS
We need to select a datum and a type of projected CRS.
Projected CRS are good for local mapping. For example, state planes are used to minimize distortion within certain parts of the state. They are measured in both feet and meters.

Universal Transverse Mercator Zones divide the Earth into 60 vertical zones, each 6 degrees wide. UTM coordinates are in meters and do not have negative numbers.






Important



Say we’re checking st_crs(data) and our CRS is missing or labelled incorrectly.
We will then use st_set_crs() to set a CRS and label the CRS correctly.
To change the CRS, use st_transform(stations, 2272). Since we are using the correct units, we can then do spatial operations such as st_buffer(stations, 500)

title: Week 4: Spatial Data
text:
Spatial Analysis
Anything dealing with spatial data will have a prefix of st before the method.

Boolean operations

st_intersects(A, B) returns a boolean value on if A or B intersect.
st_touches(A, B) returns a boolean value on if A or B share a border.
st_within(A, C) returns a boolean value on if C is completely within A.



Filtering operations

st_filter() selects features based on a specified distance
st_intersection() creates a new polygon based on the overlap between two
st_union() is like st_intersection(), though it keeps the polygon boundaries within the overlap



Joining operations

st_join() performs spatial joins (ex. assigning tract attributes to each station)
st_distance() returns a matrix with the distance between every station and tract

title: Verify the Claim: NYS Median Household Income
text:
Reliability of ACY 5YE Data
While only 16 counties showed a statistically significant difference in median household income, all 62 counties showed reliable estimates through the calculation of the coefficient of variation.
Reliability thresholds follow Jurjevich et al. (2018): CV < 12% reliable, 12–40% somewhat reliable, > 40% unreliable.


Show code
reliability_table <- inc_tested %>%
  mutate(
    `cv_2015-2019` = (`moe_2015-2019` / 1.645) / `estimate_2015-2019` * 100,
    `dot_2015-2019` = case_when(
      `cv_2015-2019` < 12  ~ "🟢",
      `cv_2015-2019` <= 40 ~ "🟡",
      TRUE     ~ "🔴"
    ),
    `flag_2015-2019` = case_when(
      `cv_2015-2019` < 12  ~ "Reliable",
      `cv_2015-2019` <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE     ~ "Unreliable"
    ),
    NAME = str_remove(NAME, " County, New York"),
    `cv_2020-2024` = (`moe_2020-2024` / 1.645) / `estimate_2020-2024` * 100,
    `dot_2020-2024` = case_when(
      `cv_2020-2024` < 12  ~ "🟢",
      `cv_2020-2024` <= 40 ~ "🟡",
      TRUE     ~ "🔴"
    ),
    `flag_2020-2024` = case_when(
      `cv_2020-2024` < 12  ~ "Reliable",
      `cv_2020-2024` <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE     ~ "Unreliable"
    ),
  ) %>%
  arrange(NAME) %>%
  select(`dot_2015-2019`, `dot_2020-2024`, NAME, `estimate_2015-2019`, `estimate_2020-2024`, `moe_2015-2019`, `moe_2020-2024`, `cv_2015-2019`, `cv_2020-2024`, `flag_2015-2019`, `flag_2020-2024`)

Conclusion
The report by the NYS Comptroller makes several statistically defensible claims, notably that many counties indeed saw a decrease in median household income between 2019 and 2024. The counties the report names with the highest decrease (Rockland and Chemung) and increase (Greene and Ulster) were all statistically significant with 90% confidence. Furthermore, all counties featured reliable ACS 5-year Estimate data.
The article falls short in mentioning the lack of statistical significance in all but 16 counties. While the report features a map of all 62 counties and their % change for each, it neglects to note how most of the counties in New York featured differences likely the artefact of sampling noise.
Disclaimer: while the differences were examined using an inflation adjustment of 1.231, exact methodological replication cannot be determined without the precise calculations used in the original report.
